files.data_silos.yaml:
# data_silos.yaml  (acme_corp-specific -- where your data physically lives)
#
# Named data-silo instances. Each object type in ontology_schema.yaml
# declares which of these named silos it lives in via its own `silo:`
# key -- this is what lets a deployment span more than one adapter.
# Split out of config.yaml into its own file: connection details
# (hosts, credentials, paths) are a genuinely different kind of
# configuration than operational tuning (which model, how many hops)
# -- often owned or secured differently in a real deployment -- so
# they get their own file, matching this project's existing "one file
# per concern" convention (ontology_schema.yaml for the data model,
# policy.yaml for RBAC/MAC).

data_silos:
  primary_sql:
    adapter: sqlite
    connection:
      path: "dev_fixtures/mediator.db"
files.ontology_schema.yaml:
# ontology_schema.yaml  (this deployment's object model)
#
# Declares what data EXISTS and how it's structured -- it does NOT by
# itself make anything visible to the LLM. Every field listed here,
# including each object type's own id_field, needs a matching
# read:<Type>.<field> grant in policy.yaml before any user can ever see
# it. A field declared here with no matching grant anywhere simply
# never appears to the LLM at all -- see core/ontology/mediator.py's
# visible_schema() docstring for the full reasoning.
#
# Each type's "storage" key holds ONLY its physical backing (which
# silo/table/id_column) -- everything else in a type's entry is purely
# SEMANTIC (what it means, how it relates to other types). Keeping
# these visibly separate means editing what a Customer IS never
# requires also understanding SQL table names, and vice versa -- see
# core/ontology/mediator.py's own docstring for the full reasoning.

object_types:
  Customer:
    storage:
      silo: primary_sql
      table: customers
      id_column: customer_id
    id_field: customer_id
    security:
      field: region
    fields:
      region:
        type: data
      name:
        type: data
      email:
        type: data
      transactions:
        type: link
        target: Transaction
        cardinality: many
        via_table: transactions
        via_column: customer_id
  Transaction:
    storage:
      silo: primary_sql
      table: transactions
      id_column: transaction_id
    id_field: transaction_id
    security:
      via_field: customer_id
    fields:
      amount:
        type: data
        # Money, so two places -- and the ontology is the only thing
        # that knows that. A UI cannot infer it: the same `number` type
        # carries a coordinate, a count and a ratio, each wanting a
        # different answer. Display only; the stored value, what an
        # action writes and what a filter compares are untouched.
        decimal_places: 2
      currency:
        type: data
      category:
        type: data
      transaction_date:
        type: data
      customer_id:
        type: link
        target: Customer
        cardinality: one

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# Action types -- the ONLY way data in this deployment is ever
# changed. Every write is a NAMED, independently-governed operation
# with its own execute: grant, its own declared parameters and its own
# declared mutations, matching Palantir Foundry's action-type model.
# There is deliberately no generic "update this field" verb.
#
# Declaring an action type here is NOT enough to make it usable: it
# also needs an execute:<ActionName> grant in policy.yaml, exactly the
# same way a field needs a read: grant. Until then it stays invisible.
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
action_types:
  RecategorizeTransactions:
    description: Change which category several transactions are filed under.
    affected_object_types: [Transaction]
    parameters:
      transaction_ids:
        type: object_reference_list
        object_type: Transaction
        required: true
        display_name: Transactions
        # PRE-FILLED ON A DETAIL PAGE, where it becomes a list of one.
        # That is what lets ONE action serve both places: the write
        # mediator expands a list into one sub-write per object, so a
        # list of one and a single reference produce the same write.
        #
        # Declaring near-identical twins -- RecategorizeTransaction and
        # RecategorizeTransactions -- put a choice in front of a person
        # that only the ontology cared about.
        default_to_current_object: true
      new_category:
        type: string
        required: true
        display_name: New category
    sub_writes:
      - object_type: Transaction
        object_id: parameter.transaction_ids
        operation: update
        mutations:
          - set:
              property: category
              value: parameter.new_category
files.policy.yaml:
# policy.yaml  (this deployment's access policy)
#
# TWO independent, both-required gates for any access (see
# core/intermediate_layer/access_control.py's check_access()):
#
#   MAC (mandatory, non-negotiable): security_attribute below names
#   which field on a user record is the row-level boundary -- a user
#   can NEVER see data outside their own value for this field, no
#   matter what role they hold.
#
#   RBAC (role-based, FULLY EXPLICIT): each user has ONE named role,
#   defined below in `roles`. Nothing is implied or inherited --
#   EVERY field a role may see needs its own listed grant, including
#   the object type's own identifier field (e.g. read:Customer.
#   customer_id) -- an identifier isn't automatically safe to expose;
#   some deployments use identifiers that are themselves sensitive
#   (a password-reset token, a verification code). A role with
#   read:Customer but zero field grants can still search/discover
#   Customer objects (if it also grants the id_field specifically) but
#   sees none of their data -- a genuinely narrower, valid capability,
#   not an error.
#
#   Action naming convention:
#     read:<Type>            -- may discover/search this type at all
#     read:<Type>.<field>     -- may see this ONE field's value
#     write:<Type>.<field>    -- may change this ONE field on an
#                                existing object (every field in a
#                                write needs its own grant --
#                                all-or-nothing for the whole write)
#     create:<Type>           -- may bring a NEW object of this type
#                                into existence (separate from any
#                                field grant -- a create also still
#                                needs write:<Type>.<field> for every
#                                field being set)
#     tool:<name>             -- may invoke this specific tool
#
# This is deliberately verbose. That verbosity is the point: nothing
# about what an LLM-driven agent can see or do on your organization's
# data should ever be implicit.

security_attribute: region

roles:
  # Deliberately minimal -- manage:users is the ONLY
  # grants an admin needs; nothing about data access is implied by
  # being able to create other users,
  # matching the fully-explicit philosophy above.
  # scripts/install.sh bootstraps the very first user with this role.
  admin:
    allowed_actions:
      - manage:users
  customer_service:
    allowed_actions:
      - read:Customer
      - read:Customer.customer_id
      - read:Customer.region
      - read:Customer.name
      - read:Customer.email
      - read:Customer.transactions
      - read:Transaction
      - read:Transaction.transaction_id
      - read:Transaction.amount
      - read:Transaction.currency
      - read:Transaction.category
      - read:Transaction.transaction_date
      - read:Transaction.customer_id
      # Without this, RecategorizeTransaction stays invisible: an
      # action type declared in ontology_schema.yaml is not usable
      # until some role is granted execute: on it by name, the same
      # way a field needs its own read: grant.
      # THE BULK SIBLING NEEDS ITS OWN GRANT, by name. Being allowed to
      # recategorise one transaction does not imply being allowed to
      # recategorise a thousand -- that is a different decision with a
      # different blast radius, and the grant vocabulary says so rather
      # than inferring it.
      - execute:RecategorizeTransactions

  # DEVELOPMENT ONLY. One login that reaches every sub-app and reads
  # every object type, so checking a layout does not mean switching
  # users three times. scripts/create_debug_user.py creates the account
  # that uses it.
  #
  # INVENTS NO PERMISSION. Every grant here is one some other role above
  # already holds, plus manage:deployment for reload testing. It is a
  # convenience, not an escalation -- but a real deployment gives each
  # role what its work needs, and an account like this has no place in
  # one. See the guard in create_debug_user.py.
  #
  # NOT KEPT IN SYNC AUTOMATICALLY: adding an object type, a field or an
  # action means adding it here too, or the debug user silently cannot
  # see it. That is the cost of explicit grants and it applies to every
  # role equally.
  debug:
    allowed_actions:
      - manage:users
      - manage:deployment
      - discover:action_types
      - read:Customer
      - read:Customer.customer_id
      - read:Customer.region
      - read:Customer.name
      - read:Customer.email
      - read:Customer.transactions
      - read:Transaction
      - read:Transaction.transaction_id
      - read:Transaction.amount
      - read:Transaction.currency
      - read:Transaction.category
      - read:Transaction.transaction_date
      - read:Transaction.customer_id
      - execute:RecategorizeTransactions

users:
  user_alice:
    region: us-west
    role: customer_service
  user_bob:
    region: us-east
    role: customer_service
  # user_carol deliberately has NO role -- she is denied every read,
  # regardless of her region matching. This is the same demonstration
  # of "MAC alone is not enough" the project has carried since RBAC was
  # first introduced -- now proven at field granularity too, not just
  # at the object-type level.
  user_carol:
    region: eu
